mappings.note: Asks why the ribbon must be cleaned: an oxide layer formed by reaction with air. That is oxidation of a metal surface in everyday handling, i.e. LO-2, not LO-1 -- the question never asks the student to classify the reaction type.
Deliverable is the equation CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 for a named substance. LO-1 (write the equation) rather than LO-2, because nothing is asked about conservation of mass.
Electrolysis of acidulated water observed in a voltameter: identifying a decomposition reaction from what is seen in the two tubes. C 1.2-LO-1 rather than C 1.3-LO-1, because no equation is demanded.
Part (iii) explicitly asks whether it is a double displacement reaction (LO-1); part (ii) asks for the balanced equation with states (C 1.3-LO-1). Both are genuinely tested, so both are cited.

Colour change of CuSO4 with an iron nail is the classic observation-to-displacement identification. Not C 1.2-LO-2: the question is about displacement, not about corrosion or rancidity, despite the stored concept tag saying 'Rusting of iron'.

Task is to identify what is oxidised and what is reduced -- exactly the oxidation/reduction half of LO-1. The referenced reactions are missing from the stored stem, but the outcome being tested is unambiguous.
Magnesium burning to MgO: decide oxidised or reduced from the observation. LO-1 covers oxidation and reduction; LO-2 would only apply if the everyday consequence were the point.
Options are all about which species is oxidised and which reduced in 2PbO + C -> 2Pb + CO2, so the redox clause of LO-1. Chose LO-1 over C 1.3-LO-1 because nothing has to be written or balanced.
Pure reaction-type classification (combination / decomposition / displacement / double displacement) -- the naming clause of LO-1 verbatim.
Predicts the products of dilute HCl on iron filings, i.e. recognising a displacement reaction. Not C 1.3-LO-1: the options are prose products, not equations.
Second half asks WHY equations must be balanced, which is the conservation-of-mass reasoning of LO-2 and not the writing skill of LO-1.
Four word-statements to be turned into balanced equations. LO-1 rather than LO-2 because the justification for balancing is not asked.
Bare instruction 'balance the following chemical equations' -- the writing/balancing outcome. The equations themselves are absent from the stored stem, but the outcome is not in doubt.
Word equations to be converted to balanced symbolic equations. Same outcome as qid:84793; the frame offers nothing finer for equation-writing drills.
Two-part demand: write the balanced equation (C 1.3-LO-1) AND name the reaction type for each (C 1.2-LO-1). Both cited because either alone would leave half the question unmapped.

Exothermic/endothermic definitions. Mapped at competency level deliberately: this frame has NO learning outcome for energy change in reactions -- LO-1 lists only combination/decomposition/displacement/double displacement/oxidation/reduction, and C 8.1-LO-1 covers only the heat SYMBOL, not the concept.
Why respiration is exothermic -- again an energy-change question with no matching LO in this frame, so it sits at competency level rather than being forced onto LO-1.
Contrasts decomposition with combination and asks for equations of each; the reaction-type discrimination is the core, so LO-1 leads over C 1.3-LO-1.
Distinguishes displacement from double displacement -- two of the six types named in LO-1. The supporting equations are illustrative, not the assessed skill.
The single instruction is 'write chemical equation involved'. C 1.3-LO-1, not C 1.2-LO-1, because the stem already tells the student it is a displacement.
Defines and exemplifies precipitation, which in this frame is the double-displacement clause of LO-1. C 8.1-LO-1 rejected: the question does not turn on the (s) symbol.
Oxidation and reduction defined by gain/loss of oxygen -- the last clause of LO-1. Not LO-2, which is about everyday consequences of oxidation.
Identify element X and the black product from a colour-change observation: an oxidation identified from observation, which is LO-1.
Painting iron to stop rust is a corrosion-in-everyday-life question, LO-2 exactly. LO-1 rejected because no reaction is to be classified.
Nitrogen flushing of oil and fat packets is the rancidity half of LO-2.
Defines corrosion and rusting with examples -- the corrosion-of-metals clause of LO-2.

Asks for the reaction of copper powder on heating (C 1.3-LO-1) and then which substance is oxidised and which reduced in the reverse reaction (C 1.2-LO-1). Figure not stored, but the stem itself names copper powder, so the outcomes are determinable.

Why H2 and Cl2 combine only in sunlight -- a question about reaction CONDITIONS and activation energy. This frame has no outcome for reaction conditions or rate, and LO-1 asks only for identification from observation, so competency level is the honest placement.
Identify X from a chain of observations and write the chemical equations of every reaction involved: equation writing (C 1.3-LO-1) plus observation-driven identification (C 1.2-LO-1).
Reactivity order deduced from four displacement reactions, and part (b) asks the nature of the reactions -- both inside the displacement clause of LO-1.
Same skill as qid:84811 with lettered elements: reads displacement reactions to rank reactivity. Mapped to the same outcome because the frame offers nothing finer for reactivity-series reasoning.
'Identify the type of reaction' (C 1.2-LO-1) and 'write chemical equations in each case' (C 1.3-LO-1) are both explicit instructions.
Deduces metals X and Y from a deposition observation and names the nature of the reaction -- displacement identified from observation, LO-1.

Physical versus chemical change. Mapped at competency level: the frame's outcomes cover reaction TYPES, equations and oxidation effects, but there is no outcome for distinguishing physical from chemical change, so forcing LO-1 would be wrong.
Classifies 4NH3 + SO2 as combustion and redox -- the oxidation/reduction clause of LO-1. C 1.3-LO-1 rejected: the equation is supplied already balanced.
Decides what is oxidised, what is reduced, and which species is the oxidising agent in 3Fe + 4H2O -- redox identification under LO-1.
Picks the exothermic processes from a list. Competency level for the same frame-gap reason as qid:84797: no energy-change outcome exists here.
Three-beaker temperature observation classified as exothermic/endothermic. Genuinely an energy-change item with no LO available, so it stays at C 1.2.
Fading of acidified KMnO4 explained as oxidation of FeSO4 -- a redox reaction identified from an observation, which is LO-1 word for word.
Selects the double displacement reaction from four equations: the double-displacement clause of LO-1, not the equation-writing outcome.
Greying of AgCl in sunlight is a decomposition identified from observation. Stored concept tag says 'Oxidation', which is wrong; the correct outcome is still LO-1 either way.

Slaking of lime judged exothermic and the resulting pH judged basic. Both halves fall outside every LO in this frame (no energy outcome, no acid-base outcome in chapter 1012's slice), so competency level.
Names the reaction type for BaCl2 + (NH4)2SO4 as both precipitation and double displacement -- LO-1 classification only; the equation is not requested.

The stem already states it is a decomposition, so nothing is left to identify; what is tested is reading the 2:1 mole ratio out of the balanced equation 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2, which belongs to the balanced-equation outcome rather than LO-1.
Endothermic-process selection -- same frame gap as qid:84818, mapped to the competency deliberately.
Chooses a soluble lead salt that will still give the double displacement with KI: applying the double-displacement clause of LO-1 to an experimental substitution.
Choice of an inert gas to stop an oil sample going rancid -- the rancidity clause of LO-2, not a reaction-type question.

Every option classifies the lab oxygen preparation as decomposition or combination, so the discriminating skill is LO-1 classification; the exothermic/endothermic rider is secondary and has no LO anyway.
Which process involves a chemical reaction at all -- a physical-versus-chemical-change item. No LO covers it, so competency level, same as qid:84815.

Turns entirely on whether (s)/(l)/(g)/(aq) are correct -- the 'states the physical states of the reactants and products' half of C 1.3-LO-1. C 8.1-LO-1 rejected because no precipitate, gas or heat symbol is being interpreted.
Selects the combination reactions from four given equations -- the combination clause of LO-1.

Blanks x and y are state labels: (s) for the PbI2 precipitate and (aq) for the dissolved salts. Writing the states is C 1.3-LO-1; recognising that the precipitate is what (s) signals is C 8.1-LO-1. Both cited because part (a) needs the precipitate reading specifically.
Four changes to be classified exothermic or endothermic -- the recurring energy-change gap in this frame, mapped at competency level.
Names the oxidising agent in six reactions, which is the oxidation/reduction clause of LO-1. No equation has to be written, so C 1.3-LO-1 does not apply.
Three balanced equations to write (C 1.3-LO-1) plus a reducing agent to identify (C 1.2-LO-1); the second instruction is welded onto the end of this stem.
'Write the chemical reaction involved and mention the type of the chemical reaction' -- one instruction per outcome, so both are cited.
Identifies thermal decomposition of FeSO4 from the smell of the gas (C 1.2-LO-1) and requires the equation (C 1.3-LO-1).

Firefly glow is the oxidation of luciferin -- an effect of oxidation met in everyday life, so LO-2 extends beyond its two named examples. LO-1 rejected: nothing is being classified into a reaction type.
Conditions for fermentation plus 'is it a chemical or a physical change'. Physical-versus-chemical change has no outcome in this frame, so competency level.
Five changes sorted into physical and chemical -- same gap as qid:84815 and qid:84830, mapped to the competency rather than forced onto LO-1.
